- HOT SPOT: a borough with a high Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents that is ALSO surrounded by other high-Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents neighboring boroughs
- COLD SPOT: a borough with a low Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents that is ALSO surrounded by other low-Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents neighboring boroughs

Look at each borough together with its neighbors from the adjacency list, and identify any that qualify. Explain your reasoning, including a computed value for each borough you name. If you test statistical significance via a permutation/randomization test, use at least 500 random shuffles -- fewer permutations can produce an unstable p-value that lands on the wrong side of the 0.05 threshold just by chance, especially when the true effect is only moderate.

1. Load both datasets (crime data and adjacency list)
2. Define thresholds for "high" and "low" crime rates (e.g., upper and lower quartiles)
3. For each borough, check its crime rate and its neighbors' crime rates
4. Identify boroughs where both the borough and all its neighbors meet the threshold criteria

# Define thresholds

low_threshold = 300

    # Get neighbor values

            neighbor_values.append(crime_df.loc[crime_df['borough'] == neighbor, 'value'].values[0])
    
    # Check if all neighbors exist in crime data
    if len(neighbor_values) == len(neighbors):
        # Check for hot spot
        if borough_value > high_threshold and all(v > high_threshold for v in neighbor_values):
            hot_spots.append((borough, borough_value))
        # Check for cold spot
        elif borough_value < low_threshold and all(v < low_threshold for v in neighbor_values):
            cold_spots.append((borough, borough_value))

print("Hot spots:", hot_spots)
